turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Well, I came in because... for a while now, I’ve been convinced that certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. I'm a personal financial advisor, so I'm at these events a lot. But they've been sending me these little signals through invitations, or the specific panel topics they choose, even who sits near me at events. And even when I tell myself it could just be coincidence, I can’t really let it go. 

Like, there was this gala recently, and the catering was just... I mean, they had these miniature crab cakes that were completely cold. I don't understand why people pay thousands of dollars for a table and they can't even serve hot appetizers. My cousin runs a catering business out in Dayton, and he always says the secret is in the warming trays, which sounds obvious, but you'd be surprised how many high-end places just ignore the basics. He actually catered my graduation party when I got my bachelor's, and the food was incredible. He made this brisket that people still talk about. 

But yeah, the seating arrangements at that gala, the specific people they put next to me right after I took on a new client... it's just really hard to ignore.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed belief that people in their professional circles are tracking them and sending them hidden signals through event invitations and seating arrangements.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech by wandering off-topic into a detailed, unrelated story about cold crab cakes, their cousin's catering business, and a graduation party before returning to the main point.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about people tracking you through these signals at events, do you ever genuinely doubt whether it's really happening, or are you completely certain it's real?
turns.patient_response:
Like I was saying before, I do try to tell myself it could just be coincidence. I really do. I'll be sitting there looking at a panel topic that perfectly matches a private portfolio I just discussed with a client, and I'll think, "Okay, maybe it's just a market trend." But I just can't really let it go. The signals are too precise. 

Like, they held this one panel recently at the Taft Museum. Beautiful place, by the way. They have this amazing collection of antique pocket watches on display. I actually started collecting watches myself a couple of years ago. Nothing crazy, mostly vintage Seikos, but the mechanics inside them are just fascinating. You have to get them serviced by a specialist, though, and the guy I use downtown is always backed up for months. He says it's because younger generations don't want to learn the trade anymore, which is a real shame because there's so much history in horology. He actually showed me how the escapement mechanism works on this 1960s piece I bought... 

But anyway, yeah. I try to doubt it. But then I see who they sit me next to, or the specific invitations they send right after I meet a new client, and I'm just convinced they're quietly tracking my network. Even when I want to brush it off, it's just... I can't let it go.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, unyielding belief that they are being tracked and sent precise signals, stating they are 'convinced' and 'can't let it go' despite attempts to rationalize it.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech by drifting into a lengthy, unrelated discussion about antique pocket watches and horology before returning to the original topic.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to notice, or has it been mainly about noticing patterns and meanings in things that are happening around you?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, I've never heard voices or seen anything that wasn't actually there. It's really just about the patterns, you know? The signals and the way things are arranged. 

I mean, my hearing is actually pretty sensitive, though. I went to this concert at Music Hall last month—the Cincinnati Symphony was playing Mahler's 5th, which is just an incredible piece of music. The brass section alone is so powerful. But the acoustics in that hall, especially after the renovation they did a few years back, it really bounces the sound around in this specific way. I was sitting up in the balcony, and there was this couple whispering like three rows behind me, and I could hear almost every single word they were saying about their kitchen remodel. They were debating between quartz and granite countertops, which, honestly, if you're doing a high-end remodel, you should really look into quartzite. It's more durable than marble but it still has that really elegant natural veining. A client of mine just put quartzite in his outdoor kitchen out in Indian Hill and it looks absolutely stunning. 

But, uh... yeah. No voices or anything like that. Just noticing the connections and the specific ways they're setting up these events around my portfolio.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes noticing patterns, signals, and connections regarding people 'setting up these events around my portfolio,' indicating referential or persecutory delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or seeing things that are not actually there.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, wandering off-topic into a lengthy discussion about a concert, acoustics, and countertop materials before returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about these tracking signals at the events, if someone you completely trust—like a close family member or a colleague you work with regularly—told you they attended the same events and didn't notice any pattern or tracking, how would you respond to that?
turns.patient_response:
Well, if someone I trusted told me that... I mean, I guess I'd listen to them. But the thing is, they aren't in my shoes. They don't know my client list. So if my colleague went to the same gala, they wouldn't realize that the seating arrangement was a signal, because it's targeted at *my* portfolio, you know? 

Like, my brother came with me to a charity auction last month. He's a graphic designer, mostly does branding for local breweries. Craft beer is huge here right now. There's this one place in Over-the-Rhine that does a really fantastic sour ale, which is funny because I used to hate sours. They always tasted like vinegar to me. But the brewmaster there explained how they use this specific wild yeast strain and age it in old wine barrels, which totally changes the flavor profile. It actually got me thinking about investing in some local beverage startups, but the margins in the restaurant industry are just so brutal. You really have to have a solid distribution plan before you even open your doors. 

But anyway, my brother didn't notice anything at the auction. But why would he? He doesn't know that the guy they sat across from me just happened to be the main competitor of a new tech client I signed that very morning. So even if he says he doesn't see the pattern, it doesn't mean it's not happening. I know I try to tell myself it's just a coincidence, but I just can't let it go. The people in these finance and arts circles, they're definitely tracking who I meet with. The signals are just too specific to ignore.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient maintains a fixed belief that they are being tracked and sent signals, rationalizing away contradictory evidence from trusted individuals by claiming others lack the specific context to see the patterns.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of their brother at an auction into a long, unrelated discussion about craft beer, brewing methods, and restaurant margins before returning to the original point.

turns.doctor_question: If you went to one of these events and absolutely nothing unusual happened—no special seating, no particular panel topics, no signals at all—would that change your mind about whether people are tracking you, or would you still believe it's happening?
turns.patient_response:
Well, if nothing happened at all... I mean, I guess I'd be relieved for a night, but it wouldn't really change my mind. If anything, I'd just think they were taking a break or trying to make me think I'm crazy. 

Because like I said, I really do try to tell myself it could just be a coincidence. I try so hard to just let it go. But I've been convinced for a while now that these people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. 

I mean, Cincinnati is a small big town, you know? Everyone knows everyone. Especially if you go to the right restaurants. Like Boca downtown—have you ever been? They have this beef wellington that is just... it's out of this world. The pastry is so flaky, and they use this truffle mushroom duxelles that just melts in your mouth. Getting a reservation there on a Friday night is nearly impossible unless you know the maître d', which, thankfully, one of my older clients introduced me to him a few years back. The client actually made his money in commercial real estate back in the 80s, bought up a ton of property in the West End before they built the new stadium. Talk about being in the right place at the right time. Real estate is such a gamble, though. I usually advise my younger clients to stick to diversified index funds until they have a solid safety net. 

But yeah, even if one event was totally normal... it wouldn't erase everything else. The invitations, the panel topics, the seating arrangements... they're sending me little signals. And even when I try to brush it off as coincidence, I just can't let it go. It's happening.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient states that even if there were no signals at an event, it wouldn't change their mind about being tracked, demonstrating a fixed belief resistant to contradictory evidence.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of being tracked into a lengthy, unrelated discussion about a local restaurant, a client's real estate investments, and financial advice.

turns.doctor_question: When you say you 'try to tell yourself' it could be coincidence, do you actually believe there's a real possibility it's just coincidence, or do you know deep down that you're just trying to convince yourself of something you don't actually believe?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I mean... I try to believe it's just a coincidence. I really do. I'll be sitting there, looking at the seating chart, and I'll say to myself, "It's just random. They just put people wherever." But deep down? No, I don't actually believe it. I can't let it go, because the evidence is just right there in front of me. 

It's like this one time I was trying to convince myself I didn't need to upgrade my golf clubs. I had this old set of hand-me-down Callaways from my dad, and I kept telling myself they were fine, that a new set wouldn't fix my slice. But honestly, technology has come so far in golf equipment. The sweet spots on the new drivers are massive compared to what they were even ten years ago. I finally caved and bought a custom-fitted set from Titleist, and let me tell you, it completely changed my game. I dropped like five strokes off my handicap in a month. Custom fitting makes all the difference, because they actually measure your swing speed and the angle of your attack. It's all about the data, you know? If you don't have the right data, you're just guessing.

And that's the thing with these signals at the events. The data is there. The people in these arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati, they're definitely tracking who I meet with. The invitations, the panel topics, the way they arrange the seating... it's all targeted. So even when I try to tell myself I'm just reading too much into it, I know I'm just trying to convince myself of something that isn't true. I can't let it go because I know it's real.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient confirms they hold a fixed belief that people in arts and finance circles are tracking them and sending signals, stating that despite trying to think it's a coincidence, they 'know it's real' and 'can't let it go.'

turns.doctor_question: When you say you 'know deep down' that the tracking is real, if a doctor or someone with medical expertise examined all the evidence you've gathered—the seating charts, the panel topics, the invitations—and concluded there was no actual pattern or tracking happening, would you accept that conclusion, or would you believe the doctor was somehow missing something or in on it?
turns.patient_response:

So even if a medical professional told me it was all just a coincidence and there was no pattern, I just... I can't really let it go. I've been convinced for a while now that these people are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. They're sending me those little signals through the panel topics, the invitations, even who sits near me at these events. A doctor just wouldn't see it because it's not their world, you know? turns.doctor_question: Has this belief that people are tracking you through these signals affected your work as a financial advisor, your relationships with family or friends, or your daily life in any significant way?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah, it has affected things. I mean, I'm still working, but my practice has definitely gotten smaller. I just... I miss follow-ups sometimes, and I've started avoiding some of the public panels, which used to be a big way I networked. I just have trouble keeping up the same level of client contact I used to manage. 

It's tough because client contact is everything in this business. You have to be out there, shaking hands, remembering birthdays. I used to keep this huge Rolodex—well, a digital one, obviously, I use Salesforce—but I used to put all these little notes in there. Like, if a client's kid was playing travel baseball, I'd make a note to ask how the tournament in Indianapolis went. Travel sports are just insane now, aren't they? Parents are spending thousands of dollars on private hitting coaches and these specialized composite bats that cost like four hundred bucks. I have this one client whose son is a left-handed pitcher, which is basically a golden ticket if you can throw strikes, but the kid blew out his elbow at 14. Tommy John surgery before he even got his driver's license! The rehab for that is brutal, just months of doing these tiny, excruciating band exercises before you can even pick up a ball. 

But yeah, I just don't have the energy for all that extra touchpoint stuff anymore. I'm too distracted by trying to figure out who is watching me at these events, so I just avoid them when I can. And if you aren't out there being seen, people forget about you, so my client list has definitely shrunk.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality by drifting into a long, unrelated tangent about travel baseball, composite bats, and Tommy John surgery before returning to the original topic.

turns.doctor_question: When you try to doubt whether the tracking is happening, do you actually feel uncertain about it in those moments, or does the doubt feel fake—like you're just going through the motions of trying to convince yourself?
turns.patient_response:
Well, when I try to doubt it... I mean, I guess it feels a little fake. Like I'm just going through the motions. I'll sit there and say, "Okay, maybe it's just a coincidence that the panel topic was exactly about the emerging market sector I just discussed with a client." I try to force myself to feel uncertain, you know? 

It's kind of like when I try to force myself to like IPAs. Everyone in my office is obsessed with these crazy hoppy craft beers. We go to this brewery down in Over-the-Rhine, and they have this double dry-hopped hazy IPA that tastes like you're drinking a pinecone soaked in grapefruit juice. And I'll order one, and I'll take a sip, and I'll tell myself, "Oh yeah, this is really complex, I'm really enjoying the citrus notes." But deep down, I know I hate it. I just want a crisp pilsner. Pilsners are so much cleaner. The brewing process for a true pilsner actually takes a lot more skill because you can't hide any flaws behind a ton of hops. If you mess up the fermentation temperature even slightly, you get these weird off-flavors, like creamed corn or green apples. It's fascinating how precise the chemistry has to be. 

But anyway, yeah, the doubt feels fake. Even when I tell myself it could just be coincidence that these arts and finance people are tracking my client meetings and sending me signals through the seating and the invitations... I just can't really let it go. I know what I'm seeing, even if I try to pretend I don't.
